stem: What is a strong warning sign of a business email compromise?
options: A request to change payment or wire instructions
An email asking you to confirm a meeting time
An invoice sent on the vendor's usual billing date
A routine monthly statement from a known vendor
why: Treat any change to payment instructions as suspect, whether it comes from a customer or a coworker.

flashcard.front: What is a strong warning sign of a business email compromise?
flashcard.back: A request to change payment or wire instructions

keyFact: BEC warning sign: request to change payment or wire instructions

stem: If you think you might have a fraudulent wire, when should you report it?
options: Immediately
Within 24 hours
By the end of the business week
After the customer confirms the loss
why: Report in minutes, not days. The first hour decides if the money comes back.

flashcard.front: If you think you might have a fraudulent wire, when should you report it?

stem: Why do you have multi-factor authentication (MFA) and what does it do?
options: It's a second layer of protection that requires two or more separate proofs of identity before granting access
It encrypts every email and file the bank sends so outsiders can't read them
It lets one strong password work across all of the bank's systems at once
It blocks every login attempt that comes from outside the bank's own network

flashcard.front: Why do you have multi-factor authentication (MFA) and what does it do?
flashcard.back: A second layer of protection. MFA requires two or more separate proofs of identity before granting access

keyFact: MFA: second layer of protection, two or more separate proofs of identity

stem: If you're wanting to verify wire instructions, who should you call?
options: The customer on the account, using the contact info in our system
The phone number listed in the email that requested the change
The sender of the instructions, by replying to their email
The receiving bank's general customer service line
why: Call back on a number from your own records, never one in the request.

flashcard.front: If you're wanting to verify wire instructions, who should you call?
flashcard.back: The customer on the account, using the contact info in our system

keyFact: Verify wire instructions: call the customer using contact info in our system

stem: Examiners mainly check that security procedures are written down.
why: Examiners test whether procedures are actually followed and documented, not just written down. Everyone in operations is a control.

stem: When attacks were targeted, what purpose did typos in phishing emails serve?
options: They were a filter that weeded out skeptical victims
They were a sign the attacker lacked skill
They helped the email get past spam filters
They made the email look like it came from a vendor
why: Typos were a filter, not incompetence. They weeded out skeptical victims, who weren't worth the manpower to chase.

stem: Why does every employee now get a convincing phishing email with no typos?
options: Attacking at scale is now cheap
Attacks have become smarter
Banks have stopped patching
Phishing is now legal in some places
why: The triage step is gone, not because attacks got smarter, but because attacking at scale is now cheap.

stem: Today, vendor oversight means just a contract and a SOC report.
why: That was then. Now it means explaining, in plain language, what your vendors are doing with your data.

stem: In May 2026, the FBI warned of Kali365. What is it?
options: AiTM phishing sold as a subscription
A deepfake voice-cloning app
A new strain of ATM malware
A free password-cracking tool
why: The FBI warned that Kali365 is AiTM phishing sold as a subscription: a technique anyone can rent.
keyFact: Kali365: AiTM phishing sold as a subscription

stem: Why doesn't MFA alone stop AiTM phishing?
options: The attacker steals the session token right after you pass the MFA check
The attacker guesses the MFA code before you enter it
MFA only protects logins made from inside the bank
The attacker turns off MFA from the phishing page
why: The session token is like a wristband at an event. Whoever holds it is treated as you, with no password and no MFA prompt.
keyFact: Session token: whoever holds it is treated as you, no password or MFA needed

stem: Microsoft observed payment fraud starting how soon after a session was stolen?
options: As little as five minutes
As little as five hours
About two days
About two weeks
why: Minutes, not days: Microsoft saw payment fraud start as little as five minutes after a session was stolen.
keyFact: Payment fraud after session theft: as little as 5 minutes

stem: In these campaigns, the fraudulent email that reaches the bank usually comes from a real vendor, customer, or title company, from their real mailbox.
why: Trusted by design: each compromised mailbox becomes the sender for the next round.

stem: What did a Kali365 subscription cost, per the FBI's May 2026 warning?
options: $250 a month
$350 a month
$500 a month
$25 a month
why: Kali365 ran $250 a month, with AI-written lures and token capture. A month of access to a separate AiTM kit cost $350.

stem: You shouldn't sign in from an email link, even one from someone you know.
why: In the Day 1 hook, a familiar sender's link led to an AiTM proxy that captured the session token.

stem: In the wire fraud walkthrough, how did the attacker keep the lender from noticing during the two weeks of watching?
options: Inbox rules moved emails mentioning "wire" or "confirm" to a folder she never opened
The attacker deleted her entire inbox every night
The attacker changed her password so she was locked out
The attacker forwarded her mail to a fake help desk
why: Inbox rules moved anything mentioning "wire," "confirm," or the customer's name into a folder she never opens. The only signals were an unfamiliar sign-in and a new inbox rule in the logs.

stem: What should you do with an MFA prompt or sign-in alert you didn't start?
options: Report it
Approve it to clear it
Ignore it if nothing else looks wrong
Wait to see if it happens again
why: Report sign-in alerts and MFA prompts you didn't start. Don't dismiss them.

stem: Which combination does the deck call the red flag in a wire request?
options: New instructions, urgency, and a reason not to verify
A new customer, a large amount, and a foreign bank
A typo, an unknown sender, and an attachment
An internal sender, a known thread, and a letterhead
why: Red flag: new instructions plus urgency plus a reason not to verify. Stop and verify.
keyFact: Wire request red flag: new instructions + urgency + a reason not to verify

stem: A second wire approver may sign off based on the first approver's callback.
why: In the walkthrough, the second approver relied on the first. Two approvals need two independent checks.

stem: After a wire fraud, what decides whether the money comes back?
options: The first hour
The first business day
The first two days
The first week
why: Report in minutes, not days. The first hour decides if the money comes back.
keyFact: Wire fraud recovery: the first hour decides

stem: Which of these is NOT part of the rehearsed playbook for the discovery step?
options: Alerts on impossible travel
A recall request
An IC3 report
Notifying the insurer
why: The playbook is a recall request, IC3 report, insurer, and customer, started in minutes. Impossible-travel alerts are the control for the watch step.

stem: Which control breaks the watch step, when the attacker is quietly reading mail?
options: Alerts on impossible travel
Phishing-resistant MFA and conditional access
Calling back on a number from the bank's own records
A rehearsed recall and IC3 playbook
why: The where-it-breaks table pairs the watch step with alerts on impossible travel.

stem: In the deck's where-it-breaks table, the callback step is the operations staff's job rather than mostly IT's.
why: Rows 1 and 2 (hook and watch) are mostly IT's job. Rows 3, 4, and 5 (ask, callback, discovery) are yours.

stem: Under the five habits, what is the red flag when you feel rushed?
options: Pressure to skip a step
A request sent after hours
An email with an attachment
A sender you haven't met
why: When you feel rushed, slow down. Pressure to skip a step is the red flag.

stem: If you're not sure a wire is fraudulent, wait until you're certain before reporting so you don't raise a false alarm.
why: Report fast, even if you're not sure. A false alarm costs minutes; a late report can cost the wire.
